claim: Global change has dramatic impacts on grassland diversity.
source: Global change has dramatic impacts on grassland diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general premise of the study.

claim: Human activities such as combustion of fossil fuels and intensification of agriculture are leading to global environmental changes.
source: Human activities, such as the combustion of fossil fuels and the intensification of agriculture, are leading to global environmental changes, causing increased air temperatures, altered precipitation patterns, and rising amounts of nitrogen to ecosystems (IPCC, Pörtner et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to IPCC report.

claim: Global environmental changes cause increased air temperatures, altered precipitation patterns, and rising amounts of nitrogen to ecosystems.
source: Human activities, such as the combustion of fossil fuels and the intensification of agriculture, are leading to global environmental changes, causing increased air temperatures, altered precipitation patterns, and rising amounts of nitrogen to ecosystems (IPCC, Pörtner et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to IPCC report.

claim: Global environmental changes result in more frequent extreme weather events such as droughts.
source: The consequences are more frequent extreme weather events such as droughts (Dai et al., 2018) and a growing accumulation of nitrogen in the soils (Holland et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dai et al., 2018.

claim: Global environmental changes result in growing accumulation of nitrogen in soils.
source: The consequences are more frequent extreme weather events such as droughts (Dai et al., 2018) and a growing accumulation of nitrogen in the soils (Holland et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holland et al., 2005.

claim: Drought and increased nitrogen input are known as major global change drivers.
source: Both, drought and increased nitrogen input, in turn, further influence ecosystems and climatic conditions; hence, they are known as major global change drivers (Sage, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sage, 2020.

claim: Global change causes changes in ecological communities.
source: Some of the most tremendous negative effects of global change are changes in ecological communities (Dornelas et al., 2014) and the extinction of species (Sage, 2020), whereby plant species are particularly affected due to their low mobility, with drastic consequences for the functioning of ecosystems.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dornelas et al., 2014.

claim: Global change causes extinction of species.
source: Some of the most tremendous negative effects of global change are changes in ecological communities (Dornelas et al., 2014) and the extinction of species (Sage, 2020), whereby plant species are particularly affected due to their low mobility, with drastic consequences for the functioning of ecosystems.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sage, 2020.

claim: Plant species are particularly affected by global change due to their low mobility.
source: Some of the most tremendous negative effects of global change are changes in ecological communities (Dornelas et al., 2014) and the extinction of species (Sage, 2020), whereby plant species are particularly affected due to their low mobility, with drastic consequences for the functioning of ecosystems.
evidence: This is stated as a logical connection between low mobility and susceptibility to global change effects.

claim: Low- and high-diversity plant communities significantly differ in their productivity and stability.
source: Studies in grassland biodiversity experiment have shown that low- and high-diversity plant communities significantly differ in their productivity and stability (Isbell et al., 2015; Marquard et al., 2009; Tilman et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Low-diversity communities lose productivity over time.
source: Low-diversity communities were shown to lose productivity over time, while high-diversity communities are more stable, so that plant diversity-productivity relationships become more positive over time (Cardinale et al., 2007; Meyer et al., 2016; Reich et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: High-diversity communities are more stable than low-diversity communities.
source: Low-diversity communities were shown to lose productivity over time, while high-diversity communities are more stable, so that plant diversity-productivity relationships become more positive over time (Cardinale et al., 2007; Meyer et al., 2016; Reich et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Plant diversity-productivity relationships become more positive over time.
source: Low-diversity communities were shown to lose productivity over time, while high-diversity communities are more stable, so that plant diversity-productivity relationships become more positive over time (Cardinale et al., 2007; Meyer et al., 2016; Reich et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Different development of plant-soil and plant-plant interactions at low and high diversity are assumed to be important drivers of strengthening biodiversity effects.
source: A different development of plant-soil and plant-plant interactions at low and high diversity are assumed to be the important drivers of these strengthening biodiversity effects (Eisenhauer et al., 2019; Thakur et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eisenhauer et al., 2019 and Thakur et al., 2021.

claim: At low plant diversity, accumulation of soil-borne pathogens might be responsible for lower plant community productivity.
source: At low plant diversity, an accumulation of soil-borne pathogens might be responsible for lower plant community productivity (Mommer et al., 2018; Thakur et al., 2021), while in high-diversity communities, complementarity effects among plants and an accumulation of soil-borne mutualists inhibit such negative processes, causing a higher productivity of these plant communities (Barry et al., 2019; Cardinale et al., 2007; Reich et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mommer et al., 2018 and Thakur et al., 2021.

claim: In high-diversity communities, complementarity effects among plants and accumulation of soil-borne mutualists inhibit negative processes and cause higher productivity.
source: At low plant diversity, an accumulation of soil-borne pathogens might be responsible for lower plant community productivity (Mommer et al., 2018; Thakur et al., 2021), while in high-diversity communities, complementarity effects among plants and an accumulation of soil-borne mutualists inhibit such negative processes, causing a higher productivity of these plant communities (Barry et al., 2019; Cardinale et al., 2007; Reich et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barry et al., 2019, Cardinale et al., 2007, and Reich et al., 2012.

claim: Diversity-dependent differences in abiotic conditions can influence plant community productivity.
source: Next to these biotic drivers, also diversity-dependent differences in abiotic conditions can influence plant community productivity (Barry et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barry et al., 2019.

claim: A decrease of species richness alters vegetation structure and density.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that a decrease of species richness alters the vegetation structure and density (Lorentzen et al., 2008), which in turn can have strong impacts on the availability of light, water, and nutrients for plants (Bachmann et al., 2018; Fischer et al., 2018; Lange et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lorentzen et al., 2008.

claim: Changes in vegetation structure and density can have strong impacts on the availability of light, water, and nutrients for plants.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that a decrease of species richness alters the vegetation structure and density (Lorentzen et al., 2008), which in turn can have strong impacts on the availability of light, water, and nutrients for plants (Bachmann et al., 2018; Fischer et al., 2018; Lange et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bachmann et al., 2018, Fischer et al., 2018, and Lange et al., 2019.

claim: There is empirical evidence that plant individuals at high diversity are selected for greater niche complementarity among species leading to more complete use of available resources.
source: There is empirical evidence that plant individuals at high diversity are selected for greater niche complementarity among species leading to a more complete use of available resources (Zuppinger-Dingley et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zuppinger-Dingley et al., 2014.

claim: At low plant diversity, accumulation of soil-borne pathogens may cause persistent species to adapt by producing more defense compounds.
source: At low plant diversity, in contrast, the accumulation of soil-borne pathogens may cause persistent species to adapt to this increase by producing more defense compounds.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on logical inference about adaptation to pathogen pressure.

claim: Over time, selection at low diversity could favor individuals that invest more in defense and less in growth.
source: Thus, over time selection could favor individuals that invest more in defense and less in growth, which could be measurable as lower biomass production and altered values of traits related to growth (Dietrich et al., 2020b; Lau and Lennon, 2011; Mraja et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dietrich et al., 2020b, Lau and Lennon, 2011, and Mraja et al., 2011.

claim: After four years, Lolium perenne showed genetic differentiation from the source population in the Jena Experiment.
source: For example, only four years after sowing, the grass species Lolium perenne L. showed genetic differentiation from the source population, which was probably due to genetic drift as well as genotype-specific interactions with other species in plant communities of different diversity (Nestmann et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nestmann et al., 2011.

claim: Genetic differentiation in Lolium perenne was probably due to genetic drift and genotype-specific interactions with other species.
source: For example, only four years after sowing, the grass species Lolium perenne L. showed genetic differentiation from the source population, which was probably due to genetic drift as well as genotype-specific interactions with other species in plant communities of different diversity (Nestmann et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nestmann et al., 2011.

claim: A study by van Moorsel et al., 2019 demonstrated genetic and epigenetic divergence among plants originated from monocultures or mixtures in three out of five studied species in the Jena Experiment.
source: Moreover, a recent study by van Moorsel et al., 2019 in the Jena Experiment demonstrated genetic and epigenetic divergence among plants originated either from monocultures or mixtures in three out of five studied species, suggesting rapid emergence of low-diversity and high-diversity genotypes.
evidence: Supported by citation to van Moorsel et al., 2019.

claim: Genetic and epigenetic divergence in the Jena Experiment suggests rapid emergence of low-diversity and high-diversity genotypes.
source: Moreover, a recent study by van Moorsel et al., 2019 in the Jena Experiment demonstrated genetic and epigenetic divergence among plants originated either from monocultures or mixtures in three out of five studied species, suggesting rapid emergence of low-diversity and high-diversity genotypes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic and epigenetic divergence data.

claim: A previous transplant experiment showed that some grassland species showed differences in their phenotype depending on plant history and soil environment.
source: In a previous transplant experiment in the field, it was shown that some of the studied grassland species showed differences in their phenotype depending on plant history (monoculture or mixture) and soil environment (Lipowsky et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lipowsky et al., 2011.

claim: Several greenhouse or common garden studies showed that plants selected at low or high diversity or grown with 'own' or different soil biota vary in their productivity and trait expression.
source: Several greenhouse or common garden studies came to similar conclusions, that is, that plants selected at low or high diversity or grown with 'own' or different soil biota vary in their productivity and trait expression (Hahl et al., 2020; Rottstock et al., 2017; van Moorsel et al., 2018b; Zuppinger-Dingley et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Under nitrogen addition, offspring of plants selected at high diversity produced more biomass than those selected at low diversity.
source: Under nitrogen addition, offspring of plants selected at high diversity produced more biomass than those selected at low diversity, while drought neutralized differences in biomass production.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Drought neutralized differences in biomass production between offspring of plants selected at high versus low diversity.
source: Under nitrogen addition, offspring of plants selected at high diversity produced more biomass than those selected at low diversity, while drought neutralized differences in biomass production.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Under the influence of global change drivers, soil history had species-specific effects on trait expression.
source: Moreover, under the influence of global change drivers, soil history, and to a lesser extent plant history, had species-specific effects on trait expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Under the influence of global change drivers, plant history had species-specific effects on trait expression to a lesser extent than soil history.
source: Moreover, under the influence of global change drivers, soil history, and to a lesser extent plant history, had species-specific effects on trait expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Plant diversity modulates plant-soil interactions and growth strategies of plants.
source: Our results show that plant diversity modulates plant-soil interactions and growth strategies of plants, which in turn affects plant eco-evolutionary pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's experimental data.

claim: Plant diversity affects plant eco-evolutionary pathways.
source: Our results show that plant diversity modulates plant-soil interactions and growth strategies of plants, which in turn affects plant eco-evolutionary pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's experimental data.

claim: Plants grown in soil of six-species communities tended to produce more root biomass than plants in soil of two-species communities in the control.
source: Plants grown in soil of six-species communities tended to produce more root biomass than plants in soil of two-species communities in the control (Table 2; Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Table 2 and Figure 1.

claim: Arrhenatherum elatius produced more root biomass in soil of six-species than two-species communities.
source: At species-level, Arrhenatherum elatius produced more root biomass and had higher root-shoot ratio, and Dactylis glomerata produced more shoot and total biomass in soil of six-species than two-species communities (Figures 1 and 2a; Appendix 1—Tables 1 and 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figures 1 and 2a and Appendix 1 Tables 1 and 3.

claim: Arrhenatherum elatius had higher root-shoot ratio in soil of six-species than two-species communities.
source: At species-level, Arrhenatherum elatius produced more root biomass and had higher root-shoot ratio, and Dactylis glomerata produced more shoot and total biomass in soil of six-species than two-species communities (Figures 1 and 2a; Appendix 1—Tables 1 and 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figures 1 and 2a and Appendix 1 Tables 1 and 3.

claim: Dactylis glomerata produced more shoot biomass in soil of six-species than two-species communities.
source: At species-level, Arrhenatherum elatius produced more root biomass and had higher root-shoot ratio, and Dactylis glomerata produced more shoot and total biomass in soil of six-species than two-species communities (Figures 1 and 2a; Appendix 1—Tables 1 and 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figures 1 and 2a and Appendix 1 Tables 1 and 3.

claim: Dactylis glomerata produced more total biomass in soil of six-species than two-species communities.
source: At species-level, Arrhenatherum elatius produced more root biomass and had higher root-shoot ratio, and Dactylis glomerata produced more shoot and total biomass in soil of six-species than two-species communities (Figures 1 and 2a; Appendix 1—Tables 1 and 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figures 1 and 2a and Appendix 1 Tables 1 and 3.

claim: Poa trivialis and Alopecurus pratensis did not differ significantly in biomass production dependent on soil or plant history.
source: The other two species, Poa trivialis and Alopecurus pratensis did not differ significantly in biomass production dependent on soil or plant history (Figures 1 and 2a; Appendix 1—Tables 2 and 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figures 1 and 2a and Appendix 1 Tables 2 and 4.

claim: Legacy treatments had no consistent effects across the four species on the expression of shoot, leaf, or root traits in the control.
source: Legacy treatments had no consistent effects across the four species on the expression of shoot, leaf, or root traits in the control (Appendix 1—table 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Appendix 1 table 5.

claim: Legacy treatments did not affect trait expression in Arrhenatherum elatius.
source: At species-level, legacy treatments did not affect trait expression in A. elatius (Figure 2a; Appendix 1—table 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2a and Appendix 1 table 6.

claim: Plants of Alopecurus pratensis were taller in home than in away-different soil.
source: Plants of A. pratensis were taller in home than in away-different soil and had thicker roots (higher root diameter) in six- than in two-species soil (Figure 2a; Appendix 1—table 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2a and Appendix 1 table 7.

claim: Plants of Alopecurus pratensis had thicker roots in six- than in two-species soil.
source: Plants of A. pratensis were taller in home than in away-different soil and had thicker roots (higher root diameter) in six- than in two-species soil (Figure 2a; Appendix 1—table 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2a and Appendix 1 table 7.

claim: Plants of Dactylis glomerata had higher leaf greenness when seeds originated from two-species communities.
source: Plants of D. glomerata had higher leaf greenness and stomatal conductance, when seeds originated from two-species communities (Figure 2a; Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2a and Appendix 1 table 8.

claim: Plants of Dactylis glomerata had higher stomatal conductance when seeds originated from two-species communities.
source: Plants of D. glomerata had higher leaf greenness and stomatal conductance, when seeds originated from two-species communities (Figure 2a; Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2a and Appendix 1 table 8.

claim: Plants of Poa trivialis had lower shoot nitrogen concentration in home soil than in away soil.
source: Plants of P. trivialis had lower shoot nitrogen concentration and root diameter, and higher SRL in home soil than in away soil (Figure 2a; Appendix 1—table 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2a and Appendix 1 table 9.

claim: Plants of Poa trivialis had lower root diameter in home soil than in away soil.
source: Plants of P. trivialis had lower shoot nitrogen concentration and root diameter, and higher SRL in home soil than in away soil (Figure 2a; Appendix 1—table 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2a and Appendix 1 table 9.

claim: Plants of Poa trivialis had higher SRL in home soil than in away soil.
source: Plants of P. trivialis had lower shoot nitrogen concentration and root diameter, and higher SRL in home soil than in away soil (Figure 2a; Appendix 1—table 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2a and Appendix 1 table 9.

claim: Arrhenatherum elatius had low pathogen infestation (0.8% ± 1.9% SD), mainly by rust species Puccinia graminis and Puccinia coronata.
source: We found a low pathogen infestation of A. elatius and A. pratensis (0.8% ± 1.9% (SD) and 0.1% ± 0.5%, respectively), mainly by the rust species Puccinia graminis Pers. and Puccinia coronata Corda.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Alopecurus pratensis had low pathogen infestation (0.1% ± 0.5% SD), mainly by rust species Puccinia graminis and Puccinia coronata.
source: We found a low pathogen infestation of A. elatius and A. pratensis (0.8% ± 1.9% (SD) and 0.1% ± 0.5%, respectively), mainly by the rust species Puccinia graminis Pers. and Puccinia coronata Corda.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Dactylis glomerata plants were strongly infested by mildew Blumeria graminis (3.1% ± 4.2% SD).
source: Plants of D. glomerata and P. trivialis, in contrast, were strongly infested by the mildew Blumeria graminis (DC.) Speer (3.1% ± 4.2% and 8.6% ± 16.5%, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Poa trivialis plants were strongly infested by mildew Blumeria graminis (8.6% ± 16.5% SD).
source: Plants of D. glomerata and P. trivialis, in contrast, were strongly infested by the mildew Blumeria graminis (DC.) Speer (3.1% ± 4.2% and 8.6% ± 16.5%, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Dactylis glomerata plants had lower mildew infestation when grown in home soil than in away soil.
source: Regarding legacy treatments, D. glomerata plants had a lower infestation when grown in home soil than in away soil, while mildew infestation of P. trivialis plants did not differ between legacy treatments (Figure 2a; Appendix 1—table 10).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2a and Appendix 1 table 10.

claim: Mildew infestation of Poa trivialis plants did not differ between legacy treatments.
source: Regarding legacy treatments, D. glomerata plants had a lower infestation when grown in home soil than in away soil, while mildew infestation of P. trivialis plants did not differ between legacy treatments (Figure 2a; Appendix 1—table 10).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2a and Appendix 1 table 10.

claim: Global change drivers had a strong impact on almost all response variables and explained a large portion of variance together with species ID.
source: Overall, global change drivers had a strong impact on almost all response variables, and explained a large portion of variance, together with species ID (Table 1; Figure 3b–d; Appendix 2—Tables 1–9).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Table 1, Figure 3b-d, and Appendix 2 Tables 1-9.

claim: Drought reduced shoot biomass production across all study species.
source: Compared to control plants, drought reduced shoot biomass production, which was found across all study species and at species-level (Figure 3a and d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3a and d.

claim: Drought did not have consistent effects on root biomass.
source: In contrast, drought did not have consistent effects on root biomass (Figure 3a and d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3a and d.

claim: Drought had positive impact on root biomass of Arrhenatherum elatius and Dactylis glomerata.
source: Drought had positive impact on root biomass of A. elatius and D. glomerata, while root biomass of A. pratensis decreased under drought and did not change significantly in P. trivialis (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3d.

claim: Root biomass of Alopecurus pratensis decreased under drought.
source: Drought had positive impact on root biomass of A. elatius and D. glomerata, while root biomass of A. pratensis decreased under drought and did not change significantly in P. trivialis (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3d.

claim: Root biomass of Poa trivialis did not change significantly under drought.
source: Drought had positive impact on root biomass of A. elatius and D. glomerata, while root biomass of A. pratensis decreased under drought and did not change significantly in P. trivialis (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3d.

claim: Total biomass production decreased when plants were exposed to drought.
source: Total biomass production was decreased, when plants were exposed to drought (Figure 3a and d) except for D. glomerata, where it was not different from the control (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3a and d.

claim: Total biomass of Dactylis glomerata under drought was not different from the control.
source: Total biomass production was decreased, when plants were exposed to drought (Figure 3a and d) except for D. glomerata, where it was not different from the control (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3d.

claim: Root-shoot ratios increased under drought.
source: Root-shoot ratios increased under drought (Figure 3a and d), which was found for all species except for P. trivialis (no significant change; Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3a and d.

claim: Root-shoot ratios of Poa trivialis did not significantly change under drought.
source: Root-shoot ratios increased under drought (Figure 3a and d), which was found for all species except for P. trivialis (no significant change; Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3d.

claim: Nitrogen input increased shoot, root, and total biomass across the four species.
source: Nitrogen input increased shoot, root, and thus also total biomass across the four species (Figure 3b) as well as in separate analyses of A. elatius and A. pratensis (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3b and 3e.

claim: Nitrogen input increased shoot, root, and total biomass in Arrhenatherum elatius and Alopecurus pratensis.
source: Nitrogen input increased shoot, root, and thus also total biomass across the four species (Figure 3b) as well as in separate analyses of A. elatius and A. pratensis (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3e.

claim: Plants of Dactylis glomerata and Poa trivialis did not change root biomass when fertilized.
source: Plants of D. glomerata and P. trivialis did not change root biomass when fertilized (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3e.

claim: Nitrogen input caused a decrease in root-shoot ratio in all species.
source: Nitrogen input caused a decrease in root-shoot ratio in all species (Figure 3a and e).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3a and e.

claim: When plants were treated with both global change drivers, the negative impact of drought on shoot biomass was cancelled out by the positive impact of nitrogen input.
source: When plants were treated with both global change drivers in combination, the negative impact of drought on shoot biomass was cancelled out by the positive impact of nitrogen input leading to an overall slight increase of shoot biomass (compared to control plants) that was also significant at the species-level except for A. elatius (Figure 3c and f).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3c and f.

claim: Treatment with both global change drivers led to an overall slight increase of shoot biomass compared to control plants.
source: When plants were treated with both global change drivers in combination, the negative impact of drought on shoot biomass was cancelled out by the positive impact of nitrogen input leading to an overall slight increase of shoot biomass (compared to control plants) that was also significant at the species-level except for A. elatius (Figure 3c and f).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3c and f.

claim: The combination of both global change drivers had an additive effect on root biomass production of Arrhenatherum elatius and Dactylis glomerata.
source: At species-level, the combination of both global change drivers had an additive effect on root biomass production of A. elatius and D. glomerata, that is, plants of both species showed highest root biomass when treated with both global change drivers (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3f.

claim: In Alopecurus pratensis and Poa trivialis, both global change drivers in combination decreased root biomass production.
source: In A. pratensis and P. trivialis, both global change drivers in combination decreased root biomass production (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3f.

claim: The combination of both global change drivers led to a slight increase in total biomass production across all study species and for Arrhenatherum elatius and Dactylis glomerata.
source: Taken together, the combination of both global change drivers led to a slight increase in total biomass production, across all study species and for the high-productive species A. elatius and D. glomerata, while plants of the low-productive species A. pratensis and P. trivialis had a similar total biomass production as in the control (Figure 3c and f).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3c and f.

claim: Plants of Alopecurus pratensis and Poa trivialis had similar total biomass production under combined global change drivers as in the control.
source: Taken together, the combination of both global change drivers led to a slight increase in total biomass production, across all study species and for the high-productive species A. elatius and D. glomerata, while plants of the low-productive species A. pratensis and P. trivialis had a similar total biomass production as in the control (Figure 3c and f).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3c and f.

claim: Across all study species, drought did not significantly alter growth height.
source: Across all study species, drought did not significantly alter growth height, but nitrogen input increased height (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3b and c.

claim: Nitrogen input increased growth height across all study species.
source: Across all study species, drought did not significantly alter growth height, but nitrogen input increased height (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3b and c.

claim: When treated with both global change drivers, drought canceled out the positive nitrogen input effect on height.
source: When treated with both global change drivers, drought canceled out the positive nitrogen input effect, leading to similar height of plants treated with both global change drivers and control plants (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3d.

claim: Drought and nitrogen input increased shoot nitrogen concentrations and leaf greenness, with additive effects when both global change drivers were applied together.
source: Further, drought and nitrogen input increased shoot nitrogen concentrations and leaf greenness, with additive effects when both global change drivers were applied together (Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3b-d.

claim: Drought did not influence LDMC and SLA.
source: Drought did not influence LDMC and SLA, while nitrogen input decreased LDMC and increased SLA (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3b and c.

claim: Nitrogen input decreased LDMC and increased SLA.
source: Drought did not influence LDMC and SLA, while nitrogen input decreased LDMC and increased SLA (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3b and c.

claim: When treated with both global change drivers, drought mitigated the decrease of LDMC under nitrogen input.
source: When treated with both global change drivers, drought mitigated the decrease of LDMC under nitrogen input, while the increase of SLA under nitrogen input did not change with drought (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3d.

claim: The increase of SLA under nitrogen input did not change with drought when both global change drivers were applied.
source: When treated with both global change drivers, drought mitigated the decrease of LDMC under nitrogen input, while the increase of SLA under nitrogen input did not change with drought (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3d.

claim: Stomatal conductance was increased when plants were treated with drought.
source: Stomatal conductance was increased, when plants were treated with drought, but did not change when fertilized irrespective of the drought treatment (Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3b-d.

claim: Stomatal conductance did not change when plants were fertilized irrespective of the drought treatment.
source: Stomatal conductance was increased, when plants were treated with drought, but did not change when fertilized irrespective of the drought treatment (Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3b-d.

claim: RLD decreased under drought irrespective of fertilization.
source: In terms of root traits, we found a decrease of RLD under drought (irrespective of fertilization) and an increase in root diameter under nitrogen input (irrespective of drought; Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3b-d.

claim: Root diameter increased under nitrogen input irrespective of drought.
source: In terms of root traits, we found a decrease of RLD under drought (irrespective of fertilization) and an increase in root diameter under nitrogen input (irrespective of drought; Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3b-d.

claim: In Dactylis glomerata, mildew infestation remained unchanged when treated with drought.
source: In D. glomerata, mildew infestation remained unchanged when treated with drought, but increased with nitrogen input.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: In Dactylis glomerata, mildew infestation increased with nitrogen input.
source: In D. glomerata, mildew infestation remained unchanged when treated with drought, but increased with nitrogen input.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: In Dactylis glomerata, when treated with both global change drivers, mildew infestation was as high as in fertilized plants.
source: When treated with both global change drivers, mildew infestation was as high as in fertilized plants (Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3b-d.

claim: In Poa trivialis, mildew infestation was increased under drought and when fertilized.
source: In P. trivialis, mildew infestation was increased under drought and when fertilized, while the combination of both global change drivers led to the highest mildew infestation (Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3b-d.

claim: In Poa trivialis, the combination of both global change drivers led to the highest mildew infestation.
source: In P. trivialis, mildew infestation was increased under drought and when fertilized, while the combination of both global change drivers led to the highest mildew infestation (Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 3b-d.

claim: Plants from two- and six-species communities did not differ in shoot biomass production when treated with drought.
source: Plants from two- and six-species communities did not differ in shoot biomass production when treated with drought, but plants from six-species communities treated with drought tended to produce more root biomass than plants from two-species communities across all study species (Table 2; Figure 4a, d and g).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Table 2 and Figure 4a, d, and g.

claim: Plants from six-species communities treated with drought tended to produce more root biomass than plants from two-species communities across all study species.
source: Plants from two- and six-species communities did not differ in shoot biomass production when treated with drought, but plants from six-species communities treated with drought tended to produce more root biomass than plants from two-species communities across all study species (Table 2; Figure 4a, d and g).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Table 2 and Figure 4a, d, and g.

claim: When plants were fertilized, fertilized plants originated from six-species communities had higher root and total biomass production than plants from two-species communities.
source: When plants were fertilized, we found an impact of plant history across all study species: fertilized plants originated from six-species communities had a higher root and total biomass production than plants from two-species communities (Table 2; Figure 4a and g).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Table 2 and Figure 4a and g.

claim: Fertilized Dactylis glomerata plants tended to produce more shoot and total biomass when originated from six-species communities.
source: This was also found in D. glomerata plants, which tended to produce more shoot and total biomass when originated from six-species communities (Figure 2c; Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2c and Appendix 1 table 3.

claim: In Arrhenatherum elatius, total biomass production of fertilized plants was significantly higher when plants were grown in home and away-same than in away-different soil.
source: In A. elatius, total biomass production of fertilized plants was significantly higher (and shoot biomass marginally significantly higher), when plants were grown in home and away-same than in away-different soil (Figure 2c; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2c and Appendix 1 table 1.

claim: In Alopecurus pratensis, fertilized plants grown in two-species community soil tended to produce more total biomass than in six-species community soil.
source: In A. pratensis, fertilized plants grown in two-species community soil tended to produce more total biomass than in six-species community soil (Figure 2c; Appendix 1—table 2), while fertilized P. trivialis showed no significant differences (Figure 2c; Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2c and Appendix 1 table 2.

claim: Fertilized Poa trivialis showed no significant differences in biomass production depending on legacy treatments.
source: In A. pratensis, fertilized plants grown in two-species community soil tended to produce more total biomass than in six-species community soil (Figure 2c; Appendix 1—table 2), while fertilized P. trivialis showed no significant differences (Figure 2c; Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2c and Appendix 1 table 4.

claim: When plants were treated with both global change drivers, there was no significant impact of legacy treatments on biomass production across all study species and for Arrhenatherum elatius.
source: When plants were treated with both global change drivers, the effects of nitrogen input were cancelled out or changed by drought, i.e., there was no significant impact of legacy treatments on biomass production across all study species and for A. elatius (Table 2; Figure 2d; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Table 2, Figure 2d, and Appendix 1 table 1.

claim: In Dactylis glomerata treated with both global change drivers, plants in home and away-different soil showed higher root-shoot ratios than plants in away-same soil.
source: In D. glomerata, the significant influence of plant history disappeared, but plants in home and away-different soil showed higher root-shoot ratios than plants in away-same soil (Figure 2d; Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2d and Appendix 1 table 3.

claim: Plants of Poa trivialis treated with both global change drivers tended to have higher root biomass and root-shoot ratios when grown in home than in away-same soil.
source: Plants of P. trivialis treated with both global change drivers tended to have higher root biomass and root-shoot ratios when grown in home than in away-same soil (Figure 2d; Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2d and Appendix 1 table 4.

claim: Alopecurus pratensis showed similar response to nitrogen input and treatment with both global change drivers: biomass production was higher in two- than in six-species community soil.
source: In contrast to the overall trend, A. pratensis was the only species which showed a similar response to nitrogen input and treatment with both global change drivers: the biomass production was higher in two- than in six-species community soil (for both global change drivers: significant higher root biomass and root-shoot ratios; Figure 2d; Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Figure 2d and Appendix 1 table 2.

claim: Shoot nitrogen concentration was not influenced by plant or soil history when treated with drought.
source: Shoot nitrogen concentration was not influenced by plant or soil history when treated with drought, but fertilized plants in six-species soil had higher shoot nitrogen concentrations than in two-species soil (soil history effect).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Fertilized plants in six-species soil had higher shoot nitrogen concentrations than in two-species soil.
source: Shoot nitrogen concentration was not influenced by plant or soil history when treated with drought, but fertilized plants in six-species soil had higher shoot nitrogen concentrations than in two-species soil (soil history effect).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Fertilized plants had lower shoot nitrogen concentrations in home than in away-different soil.
source: Moreover, fertilized plants had lower shoot nitrogen concentrations in home than in away-different soil (soil treatment effect).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: When plants were treated with both global change drivers, the nitrogen input effect on soil history was cancelled out by drought.
source: When plants were treated with both global change drivers, the nitrogen input effect on soil history was cancelled out by drought, while the impact of soil treatment did not: plants in home soil still had lower shoot nitrogen concentration than plants in away soil (Appendix 1—table 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Appendix 1 table 5.

claim: When plants were treated with both global change drivers, plants in home soil still had lower shoot nitrogen concentration than plants in away soil.
source: When plants were treated with both global change drivers, the nitrogen input effect on soil history was cancelled out by drought, while the impact of soil treatment did not: plants in home soil still had lower shoot nitrogen concentration than plants in away soil (Appendix 1—table 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Appendix 1 table 5.

claim: Other plant traits did not significantly differ depending on legacy treatments when plants were treated with nitrogen or drought.
source: Other plant traits (growth height, leaf greenness, LDMC, SLA, stomatal conductance, root traits) did not significantly differ depending on legacy treatments when plants were treated with nitrogen or drought (Appendix 1—table 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Appendix 1 table 5.

claim: Mildew infestation of Dactylis glomerata plants exposed to drought was higher in home than in away soil.
source: Mildew infestation of D. glomerata plants exposed to drought was higher in home than in away soil, while this drought effect was cancelled out by nitrogen input (Appendix 1—table 10).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Appendix 1 table 10.

claim: The drought effect on mildew infestation of Dactylis glomerata was cancelled out by nitrogen input.
source: Mildew infestation of D. glomerata plants exposed to drought was higher in home than in away soil, while this drought effect was cancelled out by nitrogen input (Appendix 1—table 10).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Appendix 1 table 10.

claim: Mildew infestation of Poa trivialis plants was not significantly influenced by legacy treatments, neither with nor without global change drivers.
source: Mildew infestation of P. trivialis plants was not significantly influenced by legacy treatments, neither with nor without global change drivers (Appendix 1—table 10).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, referenced in Appendix 1 table 10.

claim: Soil conditioned by multiple plant species has a more positive impact on plant growth than soil conditioned by only one or two plant species.
source: Our findings that A. elatius and D. glomerata plants in soil of high-diversity communities produce more biomass than in soil of low-diversity communities are in line with several greenhouse studies showing that soil conditioned by multiple plant species has a more positive impact on plant growth than soil conditioned by only one or two plant species (Guerrero‐Ramírez et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guerrero-Ramírez et al., 2019 and Yang et al., 2015.

claim: Plants probably suffered more from pathogens when grown in soil of low-diversity communities and/or benefitted more from interactions with soil mutualists in soil of high-diversity communities.
source: Plants probably suffered more from pathogens when grown in soil of low-diversity communities and/or benefitted more from interactions with soil mutualists in soil of high-diversity communities (Dietrich et al., 2021; Guerrero‐Ramírez et al., 2019; Schnitzer et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dietrich et al., 2021, Guerrero-Ramírez et al., 2019, and Schnitzer et al., 2011.

claim: Increasing root biomass at the expense of shoot biomass leading to higher root-shoot ratio under drought is a commonly observed strategy to avoid dehydration.
source: Individuals of A. elatius and D. glomerata increased in root biomass at the expense of shoot biomass, leading to higher root-shoot ratio under drought. This is a commonly observed strategy to avoid dehydration, which enables plants to tap water from deeper soil layers (in the field) and at the same time minimizes the water loss caused by transpiration (Eziz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eziz et al., 2017.

claim: The low-productive species had a three times higher loss of total biomass under drought than the highly-productive species.
source: Interestingly, the low-productive species had a three times higher loss of total biomass under drought (A. pratensis: –17.1%; P. trivialis: –15.3%) than the highly-productive species (A. elatius: –6.4%; D. glomerata: –5.7%, no significant loss of total biomass in D. glomerata).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: The drought resistance strategy of Arrhenatherum elatius and Dactylis glomerata is more effective than that of low-productive species.
source: Presumably, the drought resistance strategy of A. elatius and D. glomerata is more effective, which is possibly a competitive advantage under the field conditions of the Jena Experiment, explaining the dominance of these species.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the biomass data under drought.

claim: Plants decrease the cell density of shoot tissues under drought to minimize water loss, leading to an increase in the concentration of nitrogen compounds and chlorophyll.
source: Similar results were found in previous studies (Kocoń and Staniak, 2014; Rolando et al., 2015) and indicate a general strategy against drought stress: plants decrease the cell density of shoot tissues, in line with the reduction of shoot biomass to minimize the water loss, leading to an increase in the concentration of nitrogen compounds and chlorophyll (strong correlation between leaf greenness and chlorophyll concentration were found in Bachmann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kocoń and Staniak, 2014, Rolando et al., 2015, and Bachmann et al., 2018.

claim: There is a strong correlation between leaf greenness and chlorophyll concentration.
source: Similar results were found in previous studies (Kocoń and Staniak, 2014; Rolando et al., 2015) and indicate a general strategy against drought stress: plants decrease the cell density of shoot tissues, in line with the reduction of shoot biomass to minimize the water loss, leading to an increase in the concentration of nitrogen compounds and chlorophyll (strong correlation between leaf greenness and chlorophyll concentration were found in Bachmann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bachmann et al., 2018.

claim: The nitrogen-disease hypothesis indicates that nitrogen supply increases infection severity by altering leaf properties and resources for pathogens.
source: Both species showed a strong increase in mildew infestation when fertilized. This confirms the nitrogen-disease hypothesis indicating that nitrogen supply increases infection severity by altering leaf properties and resources for pathogens (Dordas, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dordas, 2008.

claim: Severe infestation by powdery mildew Blumeria graminis may have led to a decrease in rates of net photosynthesis in Dactylis glomerata and Poa trivialis.
source: In D. glomerata and P. trivialis, severe infestation by powdery mildew Blumeria graminis may have led to a decrease in rates of net photosynthesis (Hibberd et al., 1996; Mandal et al., 2009), so that the reduced amount of energy was mainly invested in shoot biomass, e.g., for a higher leaf turnover, and less in root biomass.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hibberd et al., 1996 and Mandal et al., 2009.

claim: Dominant species in the study benefitted more strongly from the combined application of global change drivers in comparison to subordinate species.
source: Obviously, dominant (or highly-productive) species in our study benefitted more strongly from the combined application of the global change drivers in comparison to subordinate (or low-productive) species.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's experimental data.

claim: Dry periods are becoming more frequent.
source: Assuming that dry periods are becoming more frequent (Ruosteenoja et al., 2017) and nitrogen deposition may steadily rise (Reay et al., 2008), our results suggest that competitive interactions change under the impact of multiple global change drivers, and subordinate species may become more severely threatened by extinction (Pugnaire et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruosteenoja et al., 2017.

claim: Nitrogen deposition may steadily rise.
source: Assuming that dry periods are becoming more frequent (Ruosteenoja et al., 2017) and nitrogen deposition may steadily rise (Reay et al., 2008), our results suggest that competitive interactions change under the impact of multiple global change drivers, and subordinate species may become more severely threatened by extinction (Pugnaire et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reay et al., 2008.

claim: Competitive interactions change under the impact of multiple global change drivers, and subordinate species may become more severely threatened by extinction.
source: Assuming that dry periods are becoming more frequent (Ruosteenoja et al., 2017) and nitrogen deposition may steadily rise (Reay et al., 2008), our results suggest that competitive interactions change under the impact of multiple global change drivers, and subordinate species may become more severely threatened by extinction (Pugnaire et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's experimental data combined with cited literature.

claim: The soil history effect disappeared in treatments with global change drivers, which may be explainable by a change in soil community structure under drought and/or nitrogen input.
source: The soil history effect, that is, the beneficial effect of soil biota from high-diversity plant communities on biomass production of control plants, disappeared in treatments with global change drivers, which may be explainable by a change in soil community structure under drought (Kaisermann et al., 2017; Pugnaire et al., 2019) and/or nitrogen input (Wei et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kaisermann et al., 2017, Pugnaire et al., 2019, and Wei et al., 2018.

claim: Drought can interrupt or change plant-soil interactions.
source: In line with our result, similar studies have shown that drought (Fry et al., 2018; Wilschut and van Kleunen, 2021) and nitrogen input (in 't Zandt, 2019) can interrupt or change plant-soil interactions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Fry et al., 2018 and Wilschut and van Kleunen, 2021.

claim: Nitrogen input can interrupt or change plant-soil interactions.
source: In line with our result, similar studies have shown that drought (Fry et al., 2018; Wilschut and van Kleunen, 2021) and nitrogen input (in 't Zandt, 2019) can interrupt or change plant-soil interactions.
evidence: Supported by citation to in 't Zandt, 2019.

claim: The offspring of individuals originated from high-diversity communities may be more efficient in allocating additional resources in increased growth.
source: Possibly plants at high diversity were selected for greater niche complementarity (Zuppinger-Dingley et al., 2014), while plants at low diversity were selected for increased defense against species-specific pathogens (Eisenhauer et al., 2019), that accumulate in low-diversity environments (Dietrich et al., 2021; van Ruijven et al., 2020). Consequently, the offspring of individuals originated from high-diversity communities may be more efficient in allocating additional resources in increased growth, explaining our results.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's experimental data combined with cited literature.

claim: Drought had a strong impact on the growth strategy of plants and can counteract positive diversity effects.
source: Interestingly, we did not find any significant plant history effect in plants treated with both global change drivers, indicating that drought had a strong impact on the growth strategy of the plants and can counteract positive diversity effects.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's experimental data.

claim: Plants may respond differently to global change drivers depending on the soil community with which they interact.
source: With our data in hand, we cannot determine the exact reason why we found the home advantage under fertilization but not under control conditions; however, our results show that plants may respond differently to global change drivers depending on the soil community with which they interact, which is consistent with previous findings (Puy et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's experimental data, supported by citation to Puy et al., 2021.

claim: Mainly soil biota and only to a lesser extent plant history play an important role in the expression of traits under the influence of global change drivers.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that mainly soil biota (soil history and soil treatment) and only to a lesser extent plant history play an important role in the expression of traits under the influence of global change drivers, which is in line with previous findings (Puy et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's experimental data, supported by citation to Puy et al., 2021.

claim: The soil biota composition is strongly associated with the physiology and morphology of plants.
source: This suggests that the soil biota composition is strongly associated with the physiology and morphology of the plants.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's experimental data.

claim: Shifts in soil biota composition due to plant species loss and/or global change driver impact can have strong effects on the response of plants to global change.
source: Therefore, shifts in soil biota composition due to plant species loss and/or global change driver impact can have strong effects on the response of plants to global change, which could further accelerate plant community change and species loss (Pugnaire et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's experimental data, supported by citations to Pugnaire et al., 2019 and Yang et al., 2021.

claim: The Jena Experiment is located in the floodplain of the Saale river near Jena, Germany.
source: Seed and soil material for our common garden experiment was collected from a long-term biodiversity experiment, the Jena Experiment, which is located in the floodplain of the Saale river near Jena (Thuringia, Germany, 50° 55′N, 11° 35′E, 130 m a.s.l.) (Roscher et al., 2004; Weisser et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Roscher et al., 2004 and Weisser et al., 2017.

claim: Before the establishment of the Jena Experiment in 2002, the site was a highly fertilized arable field used for growing wheat and vegetables from the early 1960s until 2000.
source: Before the establishment of the Jena Experiment in 2002, the site was a highly fertilized arable field, which had been used for growing wheat and vegetables from the early 1960s until 2000.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental site history.

claim: Mean annual air temperature recorded from 2007 to 2016 at the Jena Experiment site was 9.7 °C.
source: Mean annual air temperature recorded from 2007 to 2016 at the experimental site (Weather Station Jena-Saaleaue, Max-Planck-Institute for Biogeochemistry Jena, https://www.bgc-jena.mpg.de/wetter/) was 9.7 °C, and mean annual precipitation was 587 mm.
evidence: This is data from weather station measurements.

claim: Mean annual precipitation from 2007 to 2016 at the Jena Experiment site was 587 mm.
source: Mean annual air temperature recorded from 2007 to 2016 at the experimental site (Weather Station Jena-Saaleaue, Max-Planck-Institute for Biogeochemistry Jena, https://www.bgc-jena.mpg.de/wetter/) was 9.7 °C, and mean annual precipitation was 587 mm.
evidence: This is data from weather station measurements.

claim: The soil of the Jena Experiment study site is a Eutric Fluvisol.
source: The soil of the study site is a Eutric Fluvisol, whereas soil texture changes from sandy loam to silty clay with increasing distance from the river Saale.
evidence: This is a description of the soil type at the experimental site.

claim: Soil texture at the Jena Experiment site changes from sandy loam to silty clay with increasing distance from the river Saale.
source: The soil of the study site is a Eutric Fluvisol, whereas soil texture changes from sandy loam to silty clay with increasing distance from the river Saale.
evidence: This is a description of the soil characteristics at the experimental site.
